title: What Came Home
sub: Grades 1–2 · The display case · A helmet, a razor and the doughboys
objective: Students will look closely at the two objects in the exhibition’s display case, a soldier’s steel helmet and his shaving kit, and use them as clues. They will learn that the *doughboys* were ordinary young Americans who crossed the ocean to France, that their razors and helmets came home with them, and that we remember them with a red poppy and a quiet time on Veterans Day.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: Ordinary things tell big stories. A helmet and a razor show us real young men who went far from home, and what came home with them.

materials: The *Show your class* page (page 3), projected or printed
A modern razor or helmet to compare (optional)
Red crayons; differentiated handouts, one per student
questions: What is each object made of? How can you tell?
Why would a soldier need a razor so far from home?
The helmet has an emblem. When was it put there, and by whom?
If you went far away, what one thing would you take with you?
connection: **Visit the exhibition:** the helmet and the shaving kit stand in the display case. Look for the emblem on the helmet, and the little box of blades in the kit.
**Online:** each object has its own page, with a picture you can turn. Then place a poppy in *The Memorial*.

steps.title: A mystery object
script: Show the shaving kit on page 3 without naming it. *“What is it? Who do you think used it?”* Let students describe what they see: the case, the handle, the little box. Take guesses. Then: *“It is a razor, for shaving. It belonged to a soldier more than a hundred years ago. Today we find out who he was, and what came home with him.”*

steps.title: Who were the doughboys?
script: **Who were the doughboys?** Show the faces on the poster. In April 1917 America joined a very big war, the Great War. Two million young Americans crossed the Atlantic Ocean to France. *“They were farmers from Iowa, factory workers from Pittsburgh, teenagers from small Texas towns…”* They were called *doughboys*. Nobody knows for sure why: maybe because the big brass buttons on their uniforms looked like little fried-dough pastries, or maybe because marching soldiers got so dusty they looked rolled in flour.

screen.caption: They were farmers from Iowa, factory workers from Pittsburgh, teenagers from small Texas towns…

steps.purpose: Meet the doughboys: ordinary young Americans, far from home.
students: Where did the doughboys come from?
Why might they be called doughboys?

steps.title: A helmet and a razor
script: **The helmet.** Show it. It is made of steel, pressed from one piece, with a wide brim to keep a soldier’s head safe. Sand, sawdust or crushed cork was mixed into the paint so it would not shine in the light. Soldiers called it their *tin hat*. Point to the round emblem: *“This was put on after the war. Soldiers who came home started a club for veterans, the American Legion, in 1919.”*

**The shaving kit.** Every soldier was given one. Soldiers were allowed to keep their razors when they came home, and they kept shaving with them. Ask: *“What do these two things tell us about the doughboys?”*

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Match each object to what it was for, circle the right words about the doughboys, color a poppy, and draw a thing from home that tells a story.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Find the clue that shows the helmet came home, explain what came home with the soldiers, then tell the story of an object from home.

script: Ask the objectives back from the screen: *“Can you now…?”* Students show a thumb up, sideways or down. For the last, ask a Red Level student to share their clue.

steps.title: A poppy in the field
script: Open *The Memorial* and place one poppy in the field together. *“Every November, people wear a red poppy. On Veterans Day, November 11, many people keep a quiet time at 11 o’clock. That is how we remember the doughboys, and everyone who has served.”*

steps.purpose: End by remembering together, as the exhibition invites.
